The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

derivations.claim: On $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$ define the continuous periodic representative $F(y)=(2\pi y)^2$. Its normalized Fourier coefficients are $c_n=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2e^{-inx}\,dx$ after the change $x=2\pi y$. Direct integration gives $c_0=\pi^2/3$; for $n\ne0$, two integrations by parts give $c_n=2(-1)^n/n^2$ because the first boundary term cancels at $x=\pm\pi$ and $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-inx}\,dx=0$.

The normalized squared norm is $(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^4\,dx=\pi^4/5$. Under the stated Countable Choice assumption [F1], Parseval [F2] therefore gives $\pi^4/5=|c_0|^2+\sum_{n\ne0}|c_n|^2=\pi^4/9+8\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-4}$, whence $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-4}=\pi^4/90$.

For $m\ge1$ and $p=0,1,2,3$, put $J_p(m)=\int_0^\infty x^pe^{-mx}\,dx$. Direct integration gives $J_0(m)=1/m$; integration by parts on $[0,R]$ and then $R\to\infty$ gives $J_p(m)=pJ_{p-1}(m)/m$, since $R^pe^{-mR}\to0$ (for example, $e^{mR}\ge(mR)^{p+1}/(p+1)!$). Hence $J_3(m)=6/m^4$ and $J_2(m)=2/m^3$. The finite geometric identity and its limit give $(e^x-1)^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge1}e^{-mx}$ for $x>0$. The partial sums $x^3\sum_{m\le N}e^{-mx}$ are nonnegative measurable and increase pointwise; the monotone-convergence theorem [F3] for the integral defined in [F4] gives the first integral as $\sum_{m\ge1}J_3(m)=6\sum_{m\ge1}m^{-4}=\pi^4/15$.

For $0<z<1$, the geometric series is uniformly convergent on $[0,z]$, so integrating its partial sums gives $-\log(1-z)=\sum_{m\ge1}z^m/m$. At $z=e^{-x}$ the nonnegative partial sums $x^2\sum_{m\le N}e^{-mx}/m$ increase pointwise to the second integrand. Applying [F3] to the integral defined in [F4] and using step 3.1 gives its integral as $\sum_{m\ge1}J_2(m)/m=2\sum_{m\ge1}m^{-4}=\pi^4/45$. The integral ratio is therefore $1/3$.

Let $L,\beta,\hbar,c>0$ be real parameters, set $a=2\pi\hbar c/L$, and for
$n\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$ define
$$\epsilon_n=a|n|,\qquad q_n=e^{-\beta\epsilon_n},$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. For $j\ge1$, the integer max-norm shell
$$\{n\in\mathbb Z^3:|n|_\infty=j\}$$
has $24j^2+2$ points. Consequently
$$\sup_{n\ne0}q_n=e^{-\beta a}<1,\qquad \sum_{n\ne0}q_n<\infty,\qquad \sum_{n\ne0}\epsilon_n^p q_n<\infty$$
for every integer $p\ge0$. In particular, the positive mode-energy sum
$$\sum_{n\ne0}\frac{\epsilon_n}{e^{\beta\epsilon_n}-1}$$
is finite. Repeating each mode twice for two polarization labels preserves all
these conclusions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For a continuous compactly supported $h:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, the cubes $Q_{n,d}=dn+[-d/2,d/2]^3$ tile $\mathbb R^3$ up to boundaries of volume zero. Uniform continuity of $h$ bounds $|d^3\sum_nh(dn)-\int h|$ by the volume of one fixed enlarged support box times the modulus of continuity at $\sqrt3d/2$, which tends to zero. Taking $h(x)=\psi(|x|)$ proves the compactly supported radial lattice limit. To rewrite its integral when $\psi$ is signed, apply [F2] separately to the nonnegative radial functions $h_+(x)=\max(h(x),0)$ and $h_-(x)=\max(-h(x),0)$; both are continuous and compactly supported, so their integrals are finite. Subtracting the resulting identities and using $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from [F3] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}h(x)\,d^3x=4\pi\int_0^\infty r^2\psi(r)\,dr$. Omitting $n=0$ changes the sum by $d^3\psi(0)\to0$.

For $0<r\le1$, $f(r)\le1$ and $1-e^{-r}\ge r/2$, so $0\le g(r)\le C(1+|\log r|)$. Formulae [F2] and [F3] give the small-ball integral bound because, for $0<\delta\le1$, $\int_0^\delta r^2(1+|\log r|)\,dr=\delta^3(4/9+|\log\delta|/3)$. For the discrete sum with $0<d|n|\le\delta$, put $j=|n|_\infty$; then $dj\le\delta$ and $d|n|\ge dj$. Group the shells by $dj\in(\delta2^{-\ell-1},\delta2^{-\ell}]$. If such a group is nonempty, then $d\le\delta2^{-\ell}$ and its shell indices obey $j\le J_\ell:=\lfloor\delta2^{-\ell}/d\rfloor$. By [F1], the number of lattice points in shells up to $J_\ell$ is $\sum_{j\le J_\ell}(24j^2+2)\le C J_\ell^3\le C(\delta2^{-\ell}/d)^3$. Every point in the selected small-ball subset of this group has $d|n|\ge dj>\delta2^{-\ell-1}$ and $d|n|\le\delta\le1$, so its entropy value is at most $C(1+|\log\delta|+\ell)$. Multiplication by the cell volume $d^3$ bounds this group's contribution by $C\delta^3 2^{-3\ell}(1+|\log\delta|+\ell)$. Summing the convergent geometric series over $\ell\ge0$ gives $C'\delta^3(1+|\log\delta|)$ uniformly in $d$.

The function $f$ is continuous at zero since $\lim_{r\downarrow0}r/(e^r-1)=1$, and for $r\ge1$ it is bounded by $C(1+r)e^{-r}$. For $0<d\le1$ and $x\in Q_{n,d}$, $||dn|-|x||\le\sqrt3/2$. Thus, for $R\ge2$, each cube with $|dn|>R$ lies in $|x|>R-\sqrt3/2>1$, and the exponential bound yields $\sum_{|dn|>R}d^3f(d|n|)\le C'\int_{|x|>R-\sqrt3/2}(1+|x|)e^{-|x|}\,d^3x$. The integral tail tends to zero as $R\to\infty$, uniformly in $0<d\le1$. Apply step 1.1 on compact cutoffs and then this uniform tail bound to obtain the asserted $f$ limit and integrability.

For each fixed $d>0$, only finitely many lattice points have $d|n|<1$, and there are only finitely many shells with $dj<1$. On every remaining shell, $dj\ge1$, the Euclidean norm satisfies $j\le|n|\le\sqrt3j$, and the exponential bound gives $f(d|n|),g(d|n|)\le C(1+dj)e^{-dj}$. The shell count [F1] therefore bounds the shell contribution by $Cj^2(1+dj)e^{-dj}\le Cj^3(1+dj)e^{-dj}$. The comparison series converges by the ratio test, since the ratio of consecutive terms tends to $e^{-d}<1$. For $r\ge1$, $-\log(1-e^{-r})\le e^{-r}/(1-e^{-r})$, so $g(r)\le C(1+r)e^{-r}$; the cube estimate of step 2.1 then gives uniformly vanishing large-radius tails for the integral and the lattice sum. On each annulus $\delta\le|x|\le R$, $g(|x|)$ is continuous and the compact Riemann-sum argument of step 1.1 applies with a continuous radial cutoff equal to one on that annulus and zero near the origin and outside a larger ball. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ and $R\to\infty$ using the small-ball bound of step 1.2 and these tail bounds proves the $g$ limit and its finiteness.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
in the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, if for every compact $B\subset J\subset(0,\infty)$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

Fix $L,T,\hbar,c,k_B>0$ with SI units respectively metre, kelvin, joule-second, metre per second, and joule per kelvin. Let $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in inverse joules. The mathematical periodic-box mode set is $I=(\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\})\times\{1,2\}$, with two polarization labels and the enumeration by increasing max-norm shells and then lexicographic order; within each shell use lexicographic order on $(n,s)$. For $i=(n,s)$ set $\epsilon_i=\hbar c(2\pi/L)|n|$ in joules and $\omega_n=2\pi c|n|/L$ in inverse seconds. The zero wavevector is excluded and no zero-point energy is included.

Let $\Omega_B$ be the finite-support maps $m:I\to\mathbb N_0$, set $E(m)=\sum_{i\in I}\epsilon_i m_i$, and let $\mathcal H_B=\ell^2(\Omega_B,\mathbb C)$ with its occupation basis. Define the nonnegative diagonal multiplier $H$ by $(Ha)_m=E(m)a_m$ on $D(H)=\{a\in\ell^2(\Omega_B,\mathbb C):\sum_m E(m)^2|a_m|^2<\infty\}$, so $H|m\rangle=E(m)|m\rangle$. For each $\gamma>0$ in inverse joules define the bounded positive diagonal multiplier $e^{-\gamma H}$ by $e^{-\gamma H}|m\rangle=e^{-\gamma E(m)}|m\rangle$, and set $Z_L(\gamma)=\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}e^{-\gamma E(m)}$; the proof shows this sum is finite and equals the operator trace $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\gamma H})$. Set $q_n=e^{-\beta\epsilon_{(n,1)}}$, $Z_L=Z_L(\beta)$, $\rho_L=Z_L^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$, and $p_m=e^{-\beta E(m)}/Z_L$. Define the diagonal-state entropy by $S_L=-k_B\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}p_m\log p_m$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

The finite-box trace, energy and entropy are actual diagonal sums, not continuum mode integrals. The partition function $Z_L$ and occupations $q_n$ are dimensionless, $\rho_L$ has trace one, energy and $U_L$ have units joules, and $S_L$ has units joules per kelvin. The sums satisfy $Z_L=\prod_{n\ne0}(1-q_n)^{-2}<\infty$, $\rho_L$ is a positive trace-one trace-class operator, and every nonnegative integer energy moment under $\rho_L$ is finite. Moreover,
$$U_L=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_LH)=2\sum_{n\ne0}\frac{\epsilon_{(n,1)}}{e^{\beta\epsilon_{(n,1)}}-1}<\infty.$$
The entropy is
$$S_L=k_B(\log Z_L+\beta U_L)=2k_B\sum_{n\ne0}\left[-\log(1-q_n)+\frac{\beta\epsilon_{(n,1)}q_n}{1-q_n}\right]<\infty.$$

With $u_L=U_L/L^3$ and $s_L=S_L/L^3$ in joules per cubic metre and joules per kelvin per cubic metre, respectively, their thermodynamic-volume limits at fixed $T$ exist. For every continuous compactly supported $\psi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$, the limiting spectral energy measure is
$$\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{2}{L^3}\sum_{n\ne0}\frac{\hbar\omega_n}{e^{\beta\hbar\omega_n}-1}\psi(\omega_n)=\frac{\hbar}{\pi^2c^3}\int_0^\infty\frac{\omega^3\psi(\omega)}{e^{\beta\hbar\omega}-1}\,d\omega.$$
The integrated limits are
$$u=\lim_{L\to\infty}u_L=\frac{\pi^2k_B^4T^4}{15\hbar^3c^3},\qquad s=\lim_{L\to\infty}s_L=\frac{4u}{3T}.$$

In a separately specified isotropic freely streaming ray model, directions have uniform angular density $u/(4\pi)$ for energy and $s/(4\pi)$ for this coarse mode entropy on the unit sphere; each ray has velocity $c\hat n$. Define one-sided flux through a plane by integrating the outward normal velocity component over the outward hemisphere. Then $F=cu/4=\sigma T^4$ and $F_S=cs/4=(4/3)F/T$, where $F$ is in watts per square metre, $F_S$ in joules per kelvin per square metre per second, and $\sigma=\pi^2k_B^4/(60\hbar^3c^2)$ in watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth power. This is a mathematical model deduction; it does not assert an observed blackbody, an equilibration mechanism, or a horizon-emission law.

derivations.claim: Substitution of $r_H=2GM/c^2$ gives $A_H=16\pi G^2M^2/c^4$, $\kappa=c^2/(4GM)$, $T_\infty=\hbar c^3/(8\pi GMk_B)$, and $S_B(M)=4\pi k_BG M^2/(\hbar c)+S_0$. Differentiating the last expression yields $T_\infty\,dS_B/dM=c^2$.

By [F1] the effective-area power is $P=\eta A_H\sigma T_\infty^4=\eta\hbar c^6/(15360\pi G^2M^2)$. The adopted balance equation [A1] is therefore $M'=-\alpha M^{-2}$ with $\alpha=\eta\hbar c^4/(15360\pi G^2)>0$.

Along any positive solution, $(M^3)'=3M^2M'=-3\alpha$, hence the initial condition forces $M(t)^3=M_0^3-3\alpha t$. The positive cube root is differentiable and satisfies the ODE until it reaches the positive cutoff, giving the stated solution and time $\tau=(M_0^3-M_{\min}^3)/(3\alpha)$. This also proves uniqueness among positive solutions because every such solution has the same cube.
Integrating $P=-c^2M'$ from $0$ to $\tau$ gives $\int_0^\tau P\,dt=c^2(M_0-M_{\min})$. Differentiating $S_B(M(t))$ and using step 1.1 and $M'=-P/c^2$ yields $S_B'=-P/T_\infty$.

The entropy flux in [F1], multiplied by the stated area $A_{\rm eff}$, is $S_{\rm rad}'=(4/3)P/T_\infty$. Thus $(S_B+S_{\rm rad})'=P/(3T_\infty)\ge0$ and integration gives the two endpoint entropy formulas. Since $S_B(M)=4\pi k_BG M^2/(\hbar c)+S_0$ has positive quadratic coefficient and $M_0>M_{\min}>0$, its difference is positive and the offset cancels. No physical generalized-second-law conclusion follows beyond this stipulated model.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

citations.quote:
Assume the exact Planck energy and coarse entropy flux formulas of [[thm-tgr-photon-planck-flux]]. Use SI units: $G$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $c$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\hbar$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$, and $k_B$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Fix a normalization of the asymptotic time and energy reference, a dimensionless fraction $0<\eta\le1$, an initial mass $M_0>0$ in kilograms, and a cutoff $0<M_{\min}<M_0$. Let $M(t)>0$ be a $C^1$ mass function on an interval containing $0$ and its first cutoff time, with $M(0)=M_0$. For each $M>0$ define the model quantities
$$r_H=\frac{2GM}{c^2},\qquad A_H=4\pi r_H^2,\qquad \kappa=\frac{c^2}{4GM},\qquad T_\infty=\frac{\hbar c\kappa}{2\pi k_B},\qquad S_B(M)=\frac{k_Bc^3A_H}{4G\hbar}+S_0.$$
Here $r_H$ is in metres, $A_H$ in square metres, $\kappa$ is the fixed-reference inverse-length parameter in inverse metres, $T_\infty$ is in kelvins, and $S_0$ is a fixed entropy offset in joules per kelvin. Adopt an effective far-field emitter with area $A_{\rm eff}=\eta A_H$ and power $P=A_{\rm eff}\sigma T_\infty^4$ in watts, where $\sigma$ is the coefficient in [[thm-tgr-photon-planck-flux]]. Adopt the mass-balance equation $c^2M'(t)=-P(t)$, with $t$ in seconds measured by the fixed asymptotic time parameter; terminate the model at the first time $M(t)=M_{\min}$. Then the exact solution until that cutoff is
$$M(t)=(M_0^3-3\alpha t)^{1/3},\qquad \alpha=\frac{\eta\hbar c^4}{15360\pi G^2},\qquad \tau=\frac{M_0^3-M_{\min}^3}{3\alpha}.$$
The parameter $\alpha$ has units $\mathrm{kg^3\,s^{-1}}$. The model exports energy $c^2(M_0-M_{\min})$ in joules through cutoff. Define its coarse exported entropy by $S_{\rm rad}(t)=\int_0^t(4/3)P(t')/T_\infty(t')\,dt'$, in joules per kelvin. Then
$$S_B(M_0)-S_B(M_{\min})>0.$$
$$S_{\rm rad}(\tau)=\frac43[S_B(M_0)-S_B(M_{\min})].$$
$$\Delta(S_B+S_{\rm rad})=\frac13[S_B(M_0)-S_B(M_{\min})]\ge0,$$
where $\Delta(S_B+S_{\rm rad})=S_B(M_{\min})+S_{\rm rad}(\tau)-S_B(M_0)$ and $S_{\rm rad}(0)=0$. This is an exact conditional calculation in the fixed-reference effective-area model. It is not a theorem about a material patch of a null horizon, an exact time-dependent Einstein solution, quantum backreaction, reference-independent Stefan emission, or a universal generalized second law.

derivations.claim: Substituting $M_{\min}=M_0/2$ into the cutoff time gives $\tau=(1-1/8)M_0^3/(3\alpha)=(7/8)t_*$. The integrated energy is $c^2(M_0-M_0/2)=c^2M_0/2$.
The entropy decrease is $[4\pi k_BG/(\hbar c)](M_0^2-M_0^2/4)=3\pi k_BG M_0^2/(\hbar c)$, with the same $S_0$ at both endpoints cancelling.

Multiplying the decrease in step 2.1 by $4/3$ and $1/3$, respectively, gives $S_{\rm rad}(\tau)=4\pi k_BG M_0^2/(\hbar c)$ and total change $\pi k_BG M_0^2/(\hbar c)$. These are exact outputs of the defined positive-cutoff model.
